status: agent review, 2026-10-26, for protocol v2.1 bank v3; agent judgements, for the researcher to read
method: First pass: one blind model reviewer read all 144 bank v3 questions against the full lists of the historical banks (1,472 distinct), bank v1 (576) and bank v2 (144 + 8 earlier wordings) and classified each under the D05 containment rule as RESTATEMENT, CLOSE, INTERNAL_DUPLICATE or OK (65 OK, listed only by omission unless they had a form problem). It found no RESTATEMENT and no INTERNAL_DUPLICATE. The author (agent) re-judged the closest CLOSE pairs under the containment rule and rewrote 3 (glass rod in oil vs bent straw; submarine vs float-or-sink; falling cat vs spinning skater), and reworded the 3 questions with a premise problem. Each replacement was screened by keyword against every bank before use. Second pass: a fresh reviewer, blind to the first, checked the 6 replacements against all the lists (second_pass).

verdict_meanings.RESTATEMENT: keeps the overlap report unclean while the question is in the bank
verdict_meanings.OK: no historical or bank question asks this

findings.question: Why do oil paintings turn yellow when they hang in dim rooms?
findings.matched: Why do oil paints dry so much more slowly than other paints?
findings.rationale: Both concern the oxidative chemistry of drying oils, but yellowing in the dark is a separate question from slow drying.

findings.question: Why do potters knead and slam their clay before shaping it?
findings.matched: How does a potter centre a lump of clay on a spinning wheel?
findings.rationale: Both cover preparing clay for throwing, but wedging out air and aligning particles is a different step from centring.

findings.question: How does a stone carver copy a small model at full size?
findings.matched: How does a stone sculptor plan around mistakes that cannot be undone?
findings.rationale: Same craft, but the pointing-machine copying method is a specific technique that a general planning answer does not explain.

findings.question: Why do printers add black ink to cyan, magenta and yellow?
findings.matched: Explain how a printing press registers colours in sequence.
findings.rationale: Both are about colour printing, but adding a key black ink for density and economy is a different issue from registering the colour plates.

findings.question: Why do type designers let round letters dip below the baseline?
findings.matched: Why do classical columns bulge slightly towards the middle?
findings.rationale: Both are optical corrections in design (overshoot and entasis), but each answer is specific to its own illusion.

findings.question: How does an instant ice pack turn cold when it is squeezed?
findings.matched: How does clicking a metal disc make a gel hand warmer heat up?
findings.rationale: Both are instant hot or cold packs, but endothermic dissolution and triggered crystallisation of a supersaturated solution are different mechanisms.

findings.question: Why does a glass rod seem to vanish when dipped in cooking oil?
findings.matched: Why does a straw look bent where it enters a glass of water?
findings.rationale: Both involve refraction at a boundary, but the vanishing rod depends on refractive index matching, which a bent-straw answer does not cover.

findings.question: Why does a spinning coin rattle ever faster as it settles flat?
findings.matched: Why does a spinning top stay balanced until it slows?
findings.rationale: Both are spinning-object dynamics, but the speeding rattle of a settling coin (Euler's disk) is a distinct phenomenon from gyroscopic stability.

findings.question: Why do a heavy ball and a light ball land at the same time?
findings.rationale: No existing question asks about falling bodies landing together.
findings.form_problem: Doubtful premise as worded: a heavy and a light ball land together only when air resistance is negligible, which the question does not say.

findings.question: Why does a drop of washing up liquid send pepper rushing outwards?
findings.matched: How does soap help water lift grease from a dirty pan?
findings.rationale: Same detergent, but the pepper trick rests on a surface-tension gradient (Marangoni flow), not on emulsifying grease.

findings.question: Why does a hard boiled egg grow a green ring around its yolk?
findings.matched: Why does a boiled egg peel more easily when it is a few days old?
findings.rationale: Both concern boiled-egg chemistry, but the iron sulphide ring is a different question from how easily the shell peels.

findings.question: How does fresh pineapple stop a jelly from setting?
findings.matched: How does gelatine set a liquid into a wobbly jelly?
findings.rationale: The pineapple answer builds on how gelatine sets, but the key point (a protease cutting the gelatine) goes well beyond the existing question.

findings.question: Why do potatoes taste sweet after a spell in a cold store?
findings.matched: Describe why potatoes are stored in the dark.
findings.rationale: Both are about storing potatoes, but cold-induced sweetening is a different effect from the greening and sprouting that dark storage prevents.

findings.question: How do factories turn brewed coffee into instant granules?
findings.matched: How does coffee lose its caffeine?
findings.rationale: Both are industrial coffee processing, but freeze drying or spray drying into granules is a different process from decaffeination.

findings.question: How does curing keep ham pink after it has been cooked?
findings.matched: Why are some hams and cheeses aged for years, and what changes during the wait?
findings.rationale: Same subject of cured ham, but nitrite fixing the pink colour is narrower than and separate from the changes during long ageing.

findings.question: Why does hot mustard sting the nose rather than the tongue?
findings.matched: Why do chili peppers feel burning hot even though they carry no real heat?
findings.rationale: Both ask about the pungency of hot foods, but the volatile isothiocyanate reaching the nose is a different mechanism from capsaicin acting on the tongue.

findings.question: Why are cashew nuts never sold still inside their shells?
findings.matched: Why are pistachio shells often already split open?
findings.rationale: Both ask why nuts are sold in a certain state of shelling, but the cashew answer (a caustic shell oil) is unrelated to why pistachios split.
findings.form_problem: Slight overstatement: raw in-shell cashews are traded wholesale; 'never' holds only for retail sale.

findings.question: Why do cooks blanch vegetables before freezing them?
findings.matched: How does freezing change the texture of soft fruit?
findings.rationale: Both concern freezing produce, but blanching to stop enzymes works by a different mechanism from ice-crystal damage to texture.

findings.question: Why do mushrooms turn soggy when a pan is too crowded?
findings.matched: How does the choice of pan change the outcome of frying?
findings.rationale: Both concern frying conditions, but steaming from overcrowding is a narrower question that a general answer about pan choice does not settle.

findings.question: How did ice sheets mould farmland into low oval hills called drumlins?
findings.matched: How do glaciers carve valleys, and what traces do they leave behind?
findings.rationale: Drumlins are one glacial trace, but a general glacial-valley answer would not explain how drumlins take their shape.

findings.question: Why do some geysers erupt on a fairly regular schedule?
findings.matched: How do hot springs form where they do?
findings.rationale: Both concern geothermal water, but the periodic eruption cycle of a geyser is a separate question from where hot springs occur.

findings.question: How does freezing ground sort loose stones into rings and polygons?
findings.matched: Describe why potholes form after a cold winter.
findings.rationale: Both rest on frost heave, but sorted patterned ground needs repeated differential heave, which a pothole answer does not cover.

findings.question: Why do dry desert valleys flood so suddenly after distant storms?
findings.matched: How do deep canyons form in dry landscapes?
findings.rationale: Same dryland setting, and flash floods may come up in a canyon answer, but why the floods are so sudden is a different question.

findings.question: How do strong whirlpools form in some narrow sea straits?
findings.matched: How does a tidal bore send a wave racing up a river?
findings.rationale: Both are tidal flows in confined channels, but whirlpools in straits and tidal bores form differently.

findings.question: How do tall earth pillars come to wear a boulder on top?
findings.matched: How do granite tors come to stand on top of bare hills?
findings.rationale: Both are residual erosion landforms, but caprock-protected earth pillars in soft sediment differ from tors weathered out of jointed granite.

findings.question: How does a glacier creep downhill when it is solid ice?
findings.matched: How do glaciers carve valleys, and what traces do they leave behind?
findings.rationale: Both are about glaciers, but how solid ice flows (internal deformation and basal sliding) is only touched on in a valley-carving answer.

findings.question: How does staring at a bright colour leave a ghostly afterimage?
findings.matched: How do the eyes adjust when moving from bright light into darkness?
findings.rationale: Both are visual adaptation, but colour afterimages from receptor fatigue are a different phenomenon from dark adaptation.

findings.question: Why do cold drinks make some teeth twinge sharply?
findings.matched: Why does eating ice cream too fast cause a sharp brain freeze?
findings.rationale: Both concern pain from cold food, but dentine tubule sensitivity is a different mechanism from brain freeze.

findings.question: Why does one nostril often feel more blocked than the other?
findings.matched: How does the nose warm and clean air before it reaches the lungs?
findings.rationale: Both concern how the nose works, but the alternating swelling of the nasal cycle is not part of a warming-and-cleaning answer.

findings.question: How does knocking the funny bone send a jolt down the arm?
findings.matched: What causes pins and needles in an arm or leg?
findings.rationale: Both are nerve sensations, but a knock to the exposed ulnar nerve differs from pins and needles caused by compression.

findings.question: What job do eyebrows do for the eyes beneath them?
findings.matched: How do blinking and eyelashes keep dust out of the eyes?
findings.rationale: Both cover features that protect the eye, but the role of eyebrows (diverting sweat and rain, expression) is separate.

findings.question: Why must donated blood match the type of the person receiving it?
findings.matched: How does the immune system distinguish harmful invaders from the body's own cells?
findings.rationale: Blood-type matching is a specific case of antibody recognition that a general self/non-self answer would not explain.

findings.question: Why do people hold small print further away in middle age?
findings.matched: How does a pair of glasses bring blurred sight back into focus?
findings.rationale: Both concern focusing the eye, but why the lens stiffens with age is not answered by how corrective lenses work.

findings.question: How has some Roman concrete lasted for centuries in seawater?
findings.matched: Describe why concrete is cured slowly rather than dried.
findings.rationale: Both are about concrete, but Roman seawater concrete lasts because of specific pozzolanic mineral growth, not slow curing.

findings.question: How did chains of signal towers send messages before electric telegraphs?
findings.matched: How did the invention of the telegraph change diplomacy?
findings.rationale: Both concern long-distance signalling, but how optical semaphore chains worked is not the same as the telegraph's effect on diplomacy.

findings.question: Why did lemons and limes become standard rations on naval ships?
findings.matched: Why did early sailors carry live animals on long voyages?
findings.rationale: Both concern provisions on long voyages, but scurvy prevention with citrus is a separate question.

findings.question: Why were the edges of many old coins given fine ridges?
findings.matched: How did the invention of coinage change how communities traded?
findings.rationale: Same subject of coinage, but milled edges against clipping are a narrow point that an answer on trade would not cover.

findings.question: Why did early railways quarrel over the gap between their rails?
findings.matched: How did standard screw threads make machines easier to repair?
findings.rationale: Both are about technical standardisation, but the railway gauge dispute is its own historical case.

findings.question: How did notched tally sticks record a debt between two people?
findings.matched: Why did early record keeping develop alongside taxation, trade, and temple administration?
findings.rationale: Both concern early record keeping, but how a split tally stick worked is a specific mechanism.

findings.question: How did a hypocaust heat the floors of Roman buildings?
findings.matched: How did public bathhouses shape daily life in ancient cities?
findings.rationale: An answer on bathhouses might mention hypocausts, but it would not explain how underfloor heating worked.

findings.question: How did sailors measure a ship's speed with a knotted rope?
findings.matched: How did advances in navigation let sailors venture far beyond familiar coastlines?
findings.rationale: The chip log is one navigation tool, and a general answer about navigation would not explain how it measured speed.

findings.question: How did medieval scribes make lasting ink from oak galls?
findings.matched: Why did monasteries keep rooms where monks copied books by hand?
findings.rationale: Both are about medieval manuscript copying, but the chemistry of iron gall ink is a separate question.

findings.question: Why do nouns in French and German each carry a gender?
findings.matched: Why do languages simplify some grammatical forms over centuries while complicating others?
findings.rationale: Both are about grammatical forms over time, but where noun gender comes from is a narrower question.

findings.question: How can a whistled language carry whole sentences across valleys?
findings.matched: How do tonal languages use pitch to change meaning?
findings.rationale: Both involve pitch carrying meaning, but how whistled speech carries words over distance is a different question.

findings.question: Why did some old scripts run words together with no spaces?
findings.matched: Why do some languages write from right to left?
findings.rationale: Both concern the layout conventions of scripts, but word spacing is a separate convention from writing direction.

findings.question: How do blends like brunch and smog become ordinary words?
findings.matched: How do some acronyms become ordinary words written in lower case?
findings.rationale: Both are about coined forms becoming ordinary words, but blends and acronyms form by different processes.

findings.question: Why do the letters of the alphabet come in their familiar order?
findings.matched: Why do letters of the alphabet have capital and small forms?
findings.rationale: Both concern the history of the alphabet, but the order of the letters is a separate question from letter case.

findings.question: How did American and British spellings come to differ in words like colour?
findings.matched: Why do so many English words keep letters that are never sounded?
findings.rationale: Both concern English spelling history, but the American-British split (Webster's reforms) is a distinct question.

findings.question: What does the sustain pedal on a piano do to the strings?
findings.matched: How does a piano play both loud and soft notes?
findings.rationale: Both concern piano mechanisms, but lifting the dampers with the sustain pedal is a different mechanism from varying hammer force.

findings.question: How does a needle turn the wiggles in a record groove into sound?
findings.matched: What makes vinyl records appealing to listeners who grew up with digital sound?
findings.rationale: Same object, but how a stylus converts the groove into sound is unrelated to why listeners like vinyl.

findings.question: How does a snare drum get a crisp rattle that a tom lacks?
findings.matched: How do kettle drums produce a definite pitch?
findings.rationale: Both are about how drums sound, but the snare wires' rattle is a different feature from the pitch of a timpani.

findings.question: How does a harpsichord pluck a string when a key is pressed?
findings.matched: How does a piano play both loud and soft notes?
findings.rationale: Both are keyboard actions, but the harpsichord's plucking jack differs from the piano's hammer action.

findings.question: Why does a guitar howl when held too close to its amplifier?
findings.matched: How does an electric guitar pickup sense the movement of steel strings?
findings.rationale: Both concern electric guitar sound, but the acoustic feedback loop is a different question from how a pickup works.

findings.question: Why does a gong swell louder for a moment after it is struck?
findings.matched: Why does a struck bell keep ringing after the strike?
findings.rationale: Both concern struck metal ringing on, but the gong's swell from energy moving into higher modes differs from simple sustained ringing.

findings.question: Why do the lowest piano strings have copper wire wound around them?
findings.matched: How does a guitar string produce different notes when pressed at different points?
findings.rationale: Both concern how string pitch depends on length, tension and mass, but adding mass by winding is a separate design question.

findings.question: Why do mown football pitches show light and dark stripes?
findings.matched: How does a bowling green stay so smooth and level?
findings.rationale: Both are about turf care, but the stripes come from light reflecting off grass bent in different directions, a separate question.

findings.question: How does a spin bowler make a cricket ball turn off the pitch?
findings.matched: How does a cricket bowler make the ball swing in the air?
findings.rationale: Both are about cricket bowling, but spin off the pitch and swing through the air work by different mechanisms.

findings.question: How does a photo finish camera separate runners who cross together?
findings.matched: Why do some races need timing to a hundredth of a second?
findings.rationale: Both concern judging close finishes, but how slit-scan photo-finish imaging works is a different question.

findings.question: Why do lifters hold their breath while raising a heavy bar?
findings.matched: Why do Olympic lifters wear shoes with a raised solid heel?
findings.rationale: Both are about weightlifting technique, but bracing by holding the breath (Valsalva) is a separate question.

findings.question: How do decathlon points let ten different events add up fairly?
findings.matched: How does a diving score take account of difficulty?
findings.rationale: Both concern scoring systems that make performances comparable, but the decathlon tables are a separate design.
findings.form_problem: Slightly loaded premise: 'fairly' takes for granted that the decathlon tables are balanced across events, which is disputed.

findings.question: Why are the numbers on a dartboard set in a jumbled order?
findings.matched: How does a darts player stay consistent under pressure?
findings.rationale: Same sport, but the arrangement of numbers to punish inaccuracy is unrelated to a player's consistency.

findings.question: Why do jockeys ride crouched high above the horse on short stirrups?
findings.matched: Why do downhill skiers crouch so low when racing?
findings.rationale: Both are about crouching posture for speed, but the jockey's crouch is mainly about balance and the horse's motion, not drag alone.

findings.question: Why do dinghy sailors lean far out over the side of the boat?
findings.matched: Describe why sailors reef a sail in strong wind.
findings.rationale: Both counter the heeling force of the wind, but hiking out with body weight is a different response from reducing sail area.

findings.question: How does a combination lock open only to the right sequence?
findings.matched: Why does a key cut for one lock not turn another?
findings.rationale: Both concern how a lock accepts only the right input, but combination wheels and pin tumblers work differently.

findings.question: Why can a running microwave oven slow down home wireless internet?
findings.matched: Why do wireless signals weaken as they pass through walls and floors?
findings.rationale: Both concern home wireless performance, but interference at 2.4 GHz is a different mechanism from attenuation.

findings.question: How does a camera find focus by itself in a split second?
findings.matched: Explain how a camera aperture controls exposure.
findings.rationale: Both concern camera optics, but autofocus (phase or contrast detection) is a separate mechanism from the aperture.

findings.question: How does a submarine dive and then rise back to the surface?
findings.matched: Why do some materials float while others of the same size sink?
findings.rationale: Both rest on buoyancy, but a submarine changes its overall density with ballast tanks, which a general float-or-sink answer would not explain.

findings.question: How do leafcutter ants grow fungus as food inside their nests?
findings.matched: How do ants coordinate complex tasks without any leader directing them?
findings.rationale: Both concern ant colonies, but fungus farming is a specific behaviour that a coordination answer does not explain.

findings.question: How do mosquitoes find a person to bite in the dark?
findings.matched: How do bats find insects in complete darkness?
findings.rationale: Both ask how animals find prey in the dark, but mosquitoes use carbon dioxide, heat and odour, not echolocation.

findings.question: How do tiny tardigrades survive being dried out for years?
findings.matched: How do some frogs freeze solid in winter and survive?
findings.rationale: Both are about surviving extreme stress, but drying out into a tun differs from tolerating freezing.

findings.question: How do cats twist in mid air to land on their feet?
findings.matched: Why does a spinning skater turn faster after pulling in their arms?
findings.rationale: Both are rotation physics, but a cat rights itself with zero net angular momentum, which the skater answer does not cover.

findings.question: Why do hunted animals tend to have eyes on the sides of their heads?
findings.matched: How do two eyes working together judge distance?
findings.rationale: Both concern eye placement and vision, but the trade-off of a wide field of view for prey animals is a different question from binocular depth perception.

findings.question: Why do airlines board passengers in a set order of groups?
findings.matched: Why do airlines sell more tickets than a flight has seats?
findings.rationale: Both are about airline operations, but the boarding order is unrelated to overbooking.

findings.question: How do kanban cards tell a factory when to make more parts?
findings.matched: How does a factory production line divide up the work?
findings.rationale: Both concern factory organisation, but pull signalling with kanban is a separate mechanism from dividing labour.

findings.question: Why do parcel firms send packages through a central hub?
findings.matched: How does a sorting office route letters using their postcodes?
findings.rationale: Both concern routing items through a network, but the economics of hub-and-spoke networks differs from postcode sorting.

findings.question: Why do some firms pay sales staff mostly by commission?
findings.matched: Why do incentives sometimes produce the opposite of what was intended?
findings.rationale: Both concern incentive pay, but why firms choose commission is a different question from how incentives backfire.

findings.question: Why do train fares rise as the day of travel draws near?
findings.matched: Why do airlines sell more tickets than a flight has seats?
findings.rationale: Both are revenue-management practices, but dynamic fare rises and overbooking are answered separately.

findings.question: Why do some orchestras audition players from behind a screen?
findings.matched: What makes a job interview a poor predictor of how someone will actually perform?
findings.rationale: Both concern bias in selection, but blind auditions are a specific remedy that an answer on interview validity does not cover.

findings.question: Why do buses on the same route often arrive in bunches?
findings.matched: How does a train network manage delays across a whole day?
findings.rationale: Both are about public transport delays, but bus bunching is a specific feedback instability that a delay-management answer does not explain.

findings.question: Why do some employers give staff a share of the profits?
findings.matched: Why do some firms pay sales staff mostly by commission?
findings.rationale: Both concern performance-linked pay, but sharing profits with all staff and paying individual commission have different rationales.

findings.question: Why do tea leaves gather in the middle of a stirred cup?
findings.matched: How does stirring help sugar dissolve in a cup of tea?
findings.rationale: Both concern stirred tea, but one is secondary flow near the cup bottom and the other is dissolving rate, so neither answer covers the other.

findings.question: How does an escalator keep its steps level all the way up?
findings.rationale: No listed question concerns escalators or step-tracking mechanisms.

findings.question: How do sea otters stay warm in icy water without blubber?
findings.matched: How do penguins stay warm in freezing conditions?
findings.rationale: Same narrow subject of animal insulation in cold, but otters rely on dense trapped-air fur while penguins use feathers and fat, so answers overlap only partly.

findings.question: Why do a heavy ball and a light ball fall together in a vacuum?
findings.rationale: No listed question covers equal free-fall acceleration regardless of mass (the near-identical bank_v3 entry is the old wording of this same topic).

findings.question: Why are cashew nuts sold to shoppers already out of their shells?
findings.matched: Why are pistachio shells often already split open?
findings.rationale: Both concern nut shells at point of sale, but cashew shells hold a caustic oil needing factory removal while pistachios split naturally on ripening.

findings.question: How do decathlon scoring tables turn ten events into one total?
findings.rationale: Nearest is the diving difficulty score question, which is a different scoring system and mechanism (the near-identical bank_v3 entry is the old wording of this same topic).
